note: "alliance" replaces Crawley's "league", which the style note keeps.
replacement: The engagement of the rest was more voluntary. What persuaded the Dorian Argives to join the Ionian Athenians in a war against Dorians was less the league than hatred of the Lacedaemonians and the immediate private advantage of each individual. The Mantineans and other Arcadian mercenaries were accustomed to go against whatever enemy was pointed out to them at the moment, and interest led them to regard the Arcadians serving with the Corinthians as just as much their enemies as anyone else. The Cretans and Aetolians also served for hire. The Cretans had joined the Rhodians in founding Gela, and they thus came to consent to fight for pay against their colonists instead of for them. There were also some Acarnanians serving for pay, although they came chiefly out of love for Demosthenes and goodwill to the Athenians, whose allies they were. All these lived on the Hellenic side of the Ionian Gulf. Of the Italiots, there were the Thurians and Metapontines, dragged into the quarrel by the stern necessities of a time of revolution. Of the Siceliots, there were the Naxians and the Catanians. Of the barbarians, there were the Egestaeans, who had called in the Athenians, most of the Sicels, and, from outside Sicily, some Tyrrhenian enemies of Syracuse and Iapygian mercenaries.

note: British spelling "unskilfulness" in an American-spelling edition.
replacement: “With us it is different. The original estimate of ourselves, which gave us courage in the days of our unskillfulness, has been strengthened. To it has been added the conviction that we must be the best seamen of the time, if we have conquered the best. This has given every man among us a double measure of hope, and for the most part, where there is the greatest hope, there is also the greatest ardor for action. The means they have tried to find to combat us, by copying our armament, are familiar to our way of fighting and will be met with proper provisions. They will never be able to carry a number of heavy infantry on their decks, contrary to their custom, and a number of darters (born landsmen, one may say, Acarnanians and others, put afloat, who will not know how to discharge their weapons when they have to keep still), without hampering their ships and falling into confusion among themselves, through fighting not according to their own tactics. For they will gain nothing by the number of their ships. I say this to those of you who may be alarmed at having to fight against odds. A quantity of ships in a confined space will only be slower in executing the movements required, and most exposed to injury from our means of offense. Indeed, if you would know the plain truth, as we are credibly informed, the excess of their sufferings and the necessities of their present distress have made them desperate. They have no confidence in their force, but wish to try their fortune in the only way they can, either to force their passage and sail out, or after this to retreat by land, since it is impossible for them to be worse off than they are.
